subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. You learn to make a computer play sounds and short tunes, and the big idea that sits under it: a program makes an output (like a sound) when it is given an input (like pressing a key). In this unit you become musicians — not with a real drum or flute, but with code. You already know this pattern from real life — press a doorbell and it rings; flick a switch and the light comes on. There are four skills, taken straight from the textbook. Second, the headline skill, they predict the outcome of a change to an algorithm — if one step is different, what happens now? Third, they create a program that makes an output from an input — press a key or click a sprite, and a sound and a picture happen. Fourth, you learn the benefits of working with others when coding — sharing ideas, spotting mistakes, and being kind teammates.

outcomes: Predict the outcome of a simple sound algorithm by reading its steps in order.
Predict the outcome of a change to an algorithm — say what will be different when one step is changed.
Explain that a program makes an output (a sound, a picture) when it is given an input (a key press, a mouse click).
In Scratch, create a program that plays a sound and shows a picture when an input happens.
Understand that a tune is a sequence of notes in order, and that volume is how loud or quiet a sound is.
Change a program on purpose (a note, the volume, or a repeat) and check the outcome against a prediction.
Outline the benefits of working with others when creating programs.

concepts.title: Making sounds: input and output
concepts.explanation: We can make lots of sounds with our bodies. Every sound has a start and then the sound itself. On a computer it is the same: something starts the program — the input — and then a sound comes out — the output. debugging.symptom: The sound plays as soon as I open the program.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Musician”.
debugging.fix: No — the output waits for the input. The meow only plays when we press the key or click the sprite. Prove it by opening the program and waiting: nothing happens until the input.

debugging.symptom: Louder volume makes the tune faster or higher.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Musician”.
debugging.fix: No. Volume only changes how loud or quiet the sound is; the notes and speed stay the same. Play the tune at 100 percent, then 20 percent, to prove the tune is identical.

debugging.symptom: Volume 0 is a nice quiet sound.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Musician”.
debugging.fix: No — volume 0 means no sound at all, total silence. A quiet sound is a small number like 10 or 20.

debugging.symptom: The order of the notes does not matter.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Musician”.
debugging.fix: It does. A tune is a sequence, so the same notes in a different order make a different tune. Swap two notes to show it.

debugging.symptom: Changing one step changes the whole program.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Musician”.
debugging.fix: Usually only the changed step is different; the rest stays the same. When you edit a step, ask what stays the same as well as what changes.

debugging.symptom: play sound until done and start sound are the same.
debugging.cause: A common mix-up in this unit, “Be a Musician”.
debugging.fix: Play sound () until done waits for the whole sound to finish; start sound () moves on straight away, so sounds can overlap.
